“Worker bees actually do adjust pitch by wing-beat gaps; Apis mellifera shifts from 230 to 270 Hz to communicate distance. Adaptable tech if you think about it.” He hitched the strap over his shoulder and took a step toward the exit cue.

Rania watched him angle past the STAFF ONLY door, unanswered questions stacked like unpaid bills. She exhaled eucalyptus breath, tapped her phone awake, and googled “handpan G major tuning local pickup,” prepared to settle on floaty, even if it came out of a different mouth entirely.
Write a short prose story about Bartosz and Ilana.

The last fluorescent tube in the far aisle popped off as Bartosz tightened the thumbscrew on the blade guide, the thin steel still riding forward on the top wheel. He exhaled sawdust breath. “The blade’s still riding forward on the top wheel—what am I missing?”

Ilana flicked her rag across the drill-press vise without looking up. “Back the tension off half a turn, then spin the wheel by hand and watch the gullet, not the teeth. When the gullet centers, lock the tilt knob.”

He gripped the cast knob like it owed him money. “Okay, but the scale says I’m already at 110 lb. I don’t want to back off too far.”

“That cracked indicator’s decorative. Ignore it; rely on the deflection test instead. Press the blade with your thumb—three millimeters side flex is plenty.” Her voice was easy, the way someone recites a phone number they actually remember.

He pressed, watched the steel bow, nodded once. “Fine. And if it drifts again after I set the guides?”

“Raise the guide post so the bearings just clear the work, then recheck. Blade wants parallelism; once geometry’s right it usually behaves.”

He adjusted. “Just promise me one thing—do NOT recommend that aftermarket tension spring. It ate a previous blade and I’m not replacing another.”

Ilana’s mouth crooked, the closest she came to a grin. “Fair enough. American crows can remember human faces for at least five years, so if that spring wrongs you again it won’t forget.”

“Did you just compare a spring to a crow?”

“Not really. Still, corvids manufacture hooked tools from twigs to fetch grubs—smart hardware for smart problems.” She tested the guide with an index finger, found a millimeter of play, snugged it.

Bartosz lowered the post. “Look, can we stick to the saw? The back bearing’s almost touching.”

“Snug it until it spins with slight drag. Fun fact: common ravens cache meat and return to the spot months later, even under snow.” The bearing hummed under her fingertip.

He measured blade protrusion with a scrap. “Great. How much blade exposure past the guides is safe?”

“Quarter-inch max. Northwestern crows drop shellfish onto crosswalks so cars crack them—nice use of human infrastructure.”

“Got it—quarter inch. Anything else before I switch the machine on?”

“Stand to the side on start-up; a broken blade moves like a startled crow in a cornfield—fast and unpredictable.”

He stepped sideways, palm on the starter, and offered the first smile of the afternoon. “You really have birds on the brain today, huh?”

“They’re just efficient. Same as a sharp, well-tracked blade—cut clean, no wasted effort.”

He hit the button. The rubber tire purred, the blade tracked dead center, and pine dust drifted through the last square of light like small dark feathers settling.
Write a short prose story about Vaughn and Aylin.

Vaughn spotted the copper stub first, then the person who was supposed to make sense of it. He crossed the diesel-stained floor, clipboard swinging like a metronome. “Hey, you’re Aylin, right? The pipe fitting here—the copper stub bending the feed line. Do you know who put that in?”

Aylin didn’t look up from the phone. Thumb flick, pause, flick. “Maybe Facilities. Dunno. You’d have to check with them.”

Vaughn exhaled through his nose. “Facilities said to ask you. They said you okayed it yesterday.”

“Doesn’t ring a bell. Could’ve been anybody.” Aylin shifted on the pallet stack, heel dangling off the edge, already halfway to gone.

Vaughn tapped the clipboard. “It’s got your tag number on the clamp. Look, I just need to know why it’s there so I can log the pressure drop.”

“Sorry, man. I’m on break. Catch the foreman when he’s back.” The screen flashed brighter; Aylin’s jaw gave a small, satisfied pop.

“He’s not due for ten minutes. Five, if the truck pulls in early. Can we walk the line now?”

“I’m off the clock. Union rules.” Aylin tucked the phone away, lips a flat line that said Department of No.

Vaughn tasted grit between his teeth. “Fine. Can you at least tell me if the tubing is temporary, or if it’s part of the system?”

“Look, I signed off on the area, not the hardware. You need the planner.” Aylin’s shoulders rose, dismissing the whole building.

“Planner’s on leave until next week. I need the numbers today.”

“Hard luck. I’m not getting pulled into overtime.” Aylin glanced at the wide loading-bay door, eye corners scanning for the promised ride.

Vaughn let his nails click against the board. “You’re already here. I just need a guess—forty-five seconds, tops.”

“Clock’s ticking. I’ve got a ride out front.”

“One sentence. Is that copper staying, or does it come out?”

“Ask Facilities. Far as I know, everything’s set.” Aylin’s foot began a steady drum against the pallet slats.

Vaughn pointed at the kink in the line. “Everything’s not set. If I file it like this, the inspector fails the whole branch.”

“That’s your headache, not mine. Talk to the shift boss.” The phone buzzed; Aylin checked it, smile tugging.

“Shift boss pointed me to you. Circle closes in five minutes.”

Aylin slid off the pallets, vest flapping open. “Then you’d better move. I’m done here.”

Vaughn’s knuckles whitened around the pen. “So you’re saying you don’t know anything about the obstruction?”

Aylin was already walking, soles thudding a hollow rhythm on concrete. “I’m saying I’m off the clock. Have a good one.”

Warehouse doors yawned around their departing echo, daylight slicing in neat, indifferent bars across Vaughn’s half-written page while the copper stub kept its secret.
Write a short prose story about Winnie and Casimir.

The Horology Lab was down in the guts of the building where the overheard pipes rattled like mild indigestion. Winnie hunched over her bench, the half-stripped pocket watch open on its velvet like a tiny corpse in an autopsy scene. She pinched the bridge of her nose; caffeine had given up reaching her optic nerves hours ago.

"Hey Cas," she called, "I need to bump my magnification up four-fold without selling plasma. Got anything between ten and forty that doesn't need a credit check?"

Casimir glanced up from the frayed bench light he was soldering, one eyebrow lifting the way a dog’s ear flags an interesting rustle. He wiped flux off the iron and pointed a chin at the loupe rack. "Sure—try the 20× Bausch & Lomb in hole seven. Glass is clean, depth of field's friendly, and the billing code just tags it as loaned equipment."

Winnie stepped over, feet swishing on the oily tiles. She lifted the loupe; the brass barrel was warm from the rack. "Twenty will split the difference nicely. Does that one play nice with the LED ring or will I roast another bulb?" She flicked her own ring on; its cold glare turned the tabletop white.

"Should be fine—those LEDs sip current, and the loupe takes standard 30 mm threads. If you want more working distance there's a 15× in the next row."

She measured the gap with a jeweller’s caliper—click, click. "I've got eight millimetres before the pivot post; fifteen might clip. Stick with twenty unless there's a hidden catch."

Casimir’s soldering iron hissed as he set it in the stand. "No catch, but you'll get chromatic fringe at the rim; stop down the field iris a hair and the color wash goes away."

Winnie grunted acceptance; she didn’t have time for optical poetry. "Chromatic I can correct later in the stack. Right now I just need the pixels. Whatever you do, don't give me the Zeiss digital loupe—university rate just doubled and I'm already eating ramen. Let's keep that option off the table."

Casimir smiled like someone who’d once tried to expense a Friday pizza. "Got it—no Zeiss. Think of it like Northwestern crows picking territory: they'll cache tens of thousands of food items and remember every location, yet ignore the one peanut that's gotten pricey."

"Lens paper?" She tapped the loupe against her palm.

"Drawer under the moth—take what you need." He flicked a glance at the dead insect sunbathing since September. "Fun fact: American crows can recognize individual human faces for at least five years, so they know which grad student owes them peanuts."

Winnie looked up, lensing him like a suspicious gull. "Good, I'll try not to owe them. Does the loupe come with a stand or am I steady-handing this like a surgeon on espresso?"

Casimir tossed the black anodized arm onto the bench like a clumsy relay baton. "There's a weighted holder in the back—black anodized arm. Oh, and crows manufacture hooked tools from twigs to winkle beetle larvae; pretty nifty machining for no opposable thumbs."

She tested the clamp; it closed around the loupe with a polite click. "As long as the holder doesn't spring like a trap and fling my watch into the parts tray, we're golden."

"Spring's light—won’t launch anything heavier than a paperclip." He bowed the iron again. "Unlike crows when they're mobbing; a group of fifty can harass a hawk all afternoon without a single casualty."

"I'll watch for dive-bombing pliers. Thanks, Cas—I'll have the loupe back before the morning crew rolls in."

He nodded toward the high window where the drywall was already shading toward dawn. "Anytime. If you're still here at dawn, listen for the local murder—they pass the lab roof right about sunrise, trading updates on whose thesis is due."
Write a short prose story about Kofi and Linnea.

Sunset smacked the window of WXYU-FM like a cheap filter, striping the rug tiger-colored and revealing every shoe-scuff. The booth furnace-baked at eighty-one, thermostat seized in solidarity with the bureaucrats downstairs. Kofi stood on a coiled XLR, clipboard clamped like riot gear, graduate ID swinging on its lanyard. His tee clung between shoulder blades. Across the rack, Linnea perched sidelong on a rolling stool, elbows hooked round her knee, hockey duffel stamped with red tape waiting by the door. She’d punched out at 11:52; messages from someone called J. kept piling her screen.

“I’ve got this fifty-hertz hum riding the vocal no matter what gain I set,” he said, voice thin. “What’s the fastest way to kill it without swapping the preamp?”

Linnea’s shrug lifted her radio-station hoodie. “Check the ground loop first. If the hum vanishes when you flip off the overheads, run a star ground and you’re done.”

“Tried that. Also lifted pin one. Still there.” The blue LED on the USB interface kept blinking like a migraine. “Could the USB cable be pulling in RF?”

“Swap the cable or use a ferrite ring,” she said, already glancing at her phone. “Anything else, the senior tech is back tomorrow noon.”

“Affirmative, but I don’t have a spare cable rated for nine-fifty locally.” He swiped sweat off his hairline. “Whatever you do, do NOT tell me to buy the thirty-dollar Mogami.”

A smile touched one corner of her mouth, more reflex than amusement. “Bees regulate hive humidity at fifty-five percent by fanning with their wings; maybe try deflecting that electromagnetic buzz like they do moisture.”

“Funny,” he said, voice flat as the console meters. “My budget is two bucks or zero. Ferrite bead from the Makerspace drawer actually work?”

“Workers coat the hive entrance with propolis, a bee-made epoxy that blocks drafts—same principle with a clip-on bead.” She flipped the phone screen-up, thumbs hovering, broadcasting I’m almost gone.

“So a bead is a long shot; noted,” Kofi muttered, scrawling. “What about routing the gain chain lower—go straight into the interface line-in instead?”

Linnea straightened, shoulders square to the exit. “True that Apis mellifera queens emit a pheromone footprint letting every bee track her location even in total darkness—your signal wants its queen too, so keep the preamp out of the path.”

“Blackouts, queens—look, can you just tell me if the line-in will clip before we test it?”

“Drone honeybees die instantly when mating snaps their genitals—clipping can be that sudden if you feed 40 dB too hot.” She flicked her hair back, revealing a Bluetooth earbud already in place for whatever waited on the other side of the door.

“Good, so trim the input pad and risk loss of detail,” Kofi said, exhale ragged. “Thanks—guess I’ll run the test.”

Linnea zipped her duffel. “Bumblebees vibrate flowers at 250 Hz to dislodge pollen—your 50 Hz might be humming pollen off every mic cable in the rack. Worth picturing.” She tapped the handle, rolling it behind her into the hallway’s fluorescent draft, leaving Kofi with the hum in his headphones and, finally, quiet.
Write a short prose story about Anisa and Bjorn.

The fluorescents kicked, buzzed, and steadied again—one Mississippi, two Mississippi—twenty-four seconds on the nose. Anisa timed it while she waited for the elevator that never hurried. Now she stood ankle-deep in paper confetti, tote bag sweat-welded to her shoulder, eyes on the only moving thing in the basement: a walrus tattoo sliding back and forth into the shredder’s mouth.

She stepped closer. “Hey, Bjorn, right? I need a game plan for a secure purge—old billing records, HIPAA-approved, nothing iffy. Tips?”

Bjorn didn’t look up. He fed three manila folders in, watched them gag, then nudged the stack with a knuckle. “You’ll want Environmental Services. Third floor, south wing. They handle shred schedules, not me.”

The wall clock clicked, cracked glass vibrating like an angry cicada. Forty-two minutes until her ride left, forty-one until the internship ended forever. “I’ve got the forms. I need the gritty steps to ensure no breach during transition. Ten minutes, tops?”

He shrugged; earbuds danced at his collar like a warning flag. “Place papers in locked cart, attach chain-of-custody tag, cart goes to shredding vendor. Pretty standard.”

Pretty useless, she thought. “We’re bulk-deleting ten years of EOBs. Drives too. Cold storage? Overwrite sequence?”

“Talk to IT upstairs. They’re real picky about destruction protocols.”

The shredder wheezed and burped a puff of fuzzy grey paper that settled on his boots. “Right, but HIPAA says billing keeps the audit trail. Logs from your system—how do you scrub those without frying the month-end batch?”

“I only run the old papers. Anything that beeps is IT. Sorry.” He angled his shoulder, the walrus now mooning her. The elevator in the corridor dinged; he counted fourteen minutes of life left.

She refused to flinch. “Clock’s ticking—if your printer can still spit an activity report, that’s my proof of custody. Takes thirty seconds.”

“Printer jam yesterday. Supply closet’s locked. Keys went missing with facilities manager.”

She pointed at the rotary bin crammed with stripe-printed paper. “So I carry this rotary bin upstairs, log it with shipping, ignore the box that says ‘do not move’—that your plan?”

“Honestly? Label it ‘confidential shred,’ leave it by the freight elevator, let the night crew sort it out.”

“Night crew’s two guys who never sign anything. That’s not chain of custody, that’s wishful thinking.”

He flicked the last folder, wiped dust from his palms, and finally met her eyes—exit sign green glowing overhead. “Look, if HIPAA mattered down here we’d have cameras. We don’t. Upstairs does. Good luck.”

Shredder teeth rattled empty. He checked his watch: 4:45 exactly. Bjorn walked toward the stairs without another syllable. Anisa stared at the bin, the useless forms in her tote, and the hallway that smelled forever of burnt coffee, adding up what survival actually cost in a place that ran on wishful thinking and fourteen-minute men.
Write a short prose story about Zahir and Ysabel.

Zahir’s sneaker squeaks, lone sound in the cavern except for the clock click each minute. The spotlight picks out dust motes like lazy confetti above the parquet.

He pokes his head toward the half-open tech door. “Quick question—how do you make jokes not land like daggers at a wedding?”

Ysabel stands mid-coil of an XLR cable, car keys chiming against the reel. “Keep them short and propose in eight-second bursts. People clap before second-guessing.”

Zahir flips a page in the spiral notebook. Red margin scribbles scream “punchline here??”. “Yeah, but timing theory doesn’t fix tacky punchlines. Serious beats need space—how much?”

She shoulders a crate. “Talk to the DJ. He’s paid to watch crying vs laughing thresholds; I just push faders.”

The vents exhale warm-lemon carpet fumes. Zahir keeps blocking her path, palms out. “The DJ won’t dissect chord progressions—could you listen to the refrain, note where it wobbles?”

“Refrain’s outside my contract. My shift ends when the hall lights dim.” The corridor light strips snap overhead, signaling the automatic countdown.

He taps the music stand—four beats, three. “Thirty seconds of your ears before you vanish—listen for tone-jerk, that whiplash shift?”

“Try YouTube. Search ‘toast parody’: the comments section debates balance better than anyone live.” She clicks the light switch off; the stage glow recedes leaving only the safety exit’s EXIT-NOW silhouette.

“See, I tried, and the comments say ‘be sincere,’ but the sincere parts get jeered offstage at open mic.”

Ysabel scrubs at a faint ketchup stain on her T-shirt. “Open mics aren’t this crowd. Slice the sincere chunk to one hook line; trust their affection for the couple.”

Zahir chews his pen cap. “A single hook is a non-answer. Where do I relocate the vulnerable verse without sounding like filler?”

“Bridge after the gag. Audience breathes, volume drops, say the sappy thing, then stomp back to chorus. Formula since Sinatra.”

He glances at his phone screen—red battery, 15:11 showing. “Sinatra was never halfway through a poli-sci dissertation at 2 AM. The meter’s killing me—any quick hacks?”

“Read it drunk. If it still lands, sober probably will. Now I’ve got speaker cables to wrap.” She loops the last neon yellow cable over her forearm like a pirate’s rope.

Zahir pins the notebook under his chin, urgent. “Before cables—just confirm the last stanza at cadence seven’s not groan-worthy?”

“It’s groan-worthy. Rewrite it on your phone walking out; the hallway has reverb if you need to test.” Backpack strap slid onto shoulder, she tilts toward the EXIT.

“Thanks for nothing concrete. Guess guts and deadline panic will do it.”

“That’s called finishing. Good luck with the toast and the thesis. Door slams itself; I’m already gone.”

The EXIT sign blinks green; the clock jumps again. Somewhere above, groomsmen laughter spills like unsorted coins down the staircase. Zahir exhales lemon-and-carpet breath, scrawls one fresh line while the acoustics around him mutter hurry-hurry-hurry.
